To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mild hypothermia is causing significant cell swelling, which is mediated by activation of the Na(+)/H(+)-antiport, while hypothermia is not preventing cell swelling from latic acid, arachidonate and glutamate.

mild hypothermia causes significant cell swelling of glial tumor cells in vitro, and that this cell swelling cannot be prevented by hypothermia from cytotoxic agents, which are mediating cytotoxic edema in vivo.

mild (32 degreesC) hypothermia causes significant swelling of glioma cells and that this cell swelling cannot be inhibited by the agents that are mediating the cytotoxic brain edemas in cerebral trauma, cerebral ischemia and other cerebral insults.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question, whether the beneficial effect of hypothermia in acute cerebral insults is mediated by a prevention of cytotoxic brain swelling.
the question whether hypothermia is a promising therapeutic procedure to protect the brain from cytotoxic brain edemas.
the elucidation of the influence of hypothermia (27 degrees and 32 degrees C) on cell swelling of glial and neuronal cells under physiological and pathological conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the protective effect of hypothermia in the brain is most likely attributable to the inhibition of the energy consuming processes, which are responsible for the development of cytostatic brain edema.
hypothermia is not protecting against cytotoxic brain edemagenic agents in vitro.
hypothermia is not a promising approach to prevent the cytotoxic brain edemas in acute brain insults.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hypothermia is a useful tool for neuroprotection, but that it is not effective in reducing cytotoxic brain swelling.
mild hypothermia is not able to protect cells against cytotoxic brain edemas.
hypothermia in itself causes cell swelling and thus should be avoided in patients with brain edema.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hypothermia does not prevent cell swelling from cytotoxic edema-inducing agents.
hypothermia itself is causing swelling of cells, and that hypothermia is not able to prevent cytotoxic swelling of cells from other causes.
hypothermia does not protect against cytotoxic edema in vitro.
